ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A vacuum system consists of a chamber of volume $V$ connected to a vacuum pump. The pump is a cylinder with a piston that moves, with a minimum volume $V_0$ and a maximum volume $V_0 + \Delta V$, where $\Delta V \ll V$. The cylinder has an inlet valve that opens when the cylinder pressure is less than the chamber pressure and an outlet valve that opens when the cylinder pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure $P_a$. The piston moves at such a rate that gas compression/expansion is adiabatic during the pumping cycle. The gas in the chamber is ideal monatomic and remains at a fixed temperature $T_a$. Initially assume $V_0 = 0$ and no leaks.

1. a. At $t=0$ the pressure inside the chamber is $P_a$. Find an equation for the pressure at a later time $t$.
2. b. Find an expression for the temperature of the gas as it is emitted from the pump cylinder into the atmosphere. Your answer may depend on time. 
(Note: There are no mathematical expressions in the provided text to convert to LaTeX format.)
3. c. Now consider the case where $0 < V_0 < \Delta V \ll V$. Find an expression for the minimum possible pressure in the chamber, $P_{\text{min}}$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$P(t) = P_{a} e^{\frac{-Rt}{V}}$
$T_{out}(t) = T_{a} e^{\frac{2Rt}{5V}}$
$P_{\text{min}} = P_{a} \left(1+ \frac{\Delta V}{V_0}\right)^{-\gamma}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The two attached figures show the same vacuum pump system: on the left is the driving mechanism labeled motor, which drives the piston in the middle labeled cylinder through a connecting rod; inside the cylinder there is a piston plate labeled piston. The right side of the cylinder is connected through valves and piping to the large cavity on the right labeled chamber, and the cavity is marked with volume V. Near the right end of the cylinder there are two valve positions, labeled inlet and outlet respectively, where inlet is located at the connection leading to the cavity, and outlet is the exit leading to the outside. Reasoning: Let R denote the swept volume rate of the pump, that is, the equivalent volume pumped away from the cavity per unit time. First take V0=0 and no leakage. The gas in the cavity maintains temperature Ta and satisfies P(t)V = N k Ta. During time dt, the pump carries away from the cavity gas whose volume under the cavity state is R dt, so the change in molecule number is dN/dt = -P(t)R/(k Ta). From P V = N k Ta, we get V dP/dt = k Ta dN/dt, so dP/dt = -(R/V)P. Combining the initial condition P(0)=Pa gives P(t)=Pa exp(-Rt/V). For the discharged gas, when it enters the cylinder, the gas pressure is P(t) and the temperature is Ta; then it is adiabatically compressed in the cylinder until the pressure reaches atmospheric pressure Pa, when outlet opens. For a monatomic ideal gas gamma=5/3, the adiabatic relation can be written as T P^((1-gamma)/gamma)=constant, so Tout/Ta = (Pa/P(t))^((gamma-1)/gamma). Substituting P(t)=Pa exp(-Rt/V) and (gamma-1)/gamma=2/5 gives Tout(t)=Ta exp(2Rt/(5V)). When there is a finite clearance volume 0<V0<Delta V, after the previous discharge ends, gas at pressure Pa is trapped in the clearance volume V0 inside the cylinder. In the next suction stroke, this part of the gas expands adiabatically from V0 to V0+Delta V, and its lowest pressure is Pa [V0/(V0+Delta V)]^gamma. If the cavity pressure is lower than this value, then inlet no longer opens, so the minimum pressure the cavity can reach is Pmin = Pa [V0/(V0+Delta V)]^gamma = Pa(1+Delta V/V0)^(-gamma).

method.method_draft: Use a continuous flow-rate balance. First read the image as a motor-driven piston cylinder connected to a chamber labeled V, with an inlet valve between chamber and cylinder and a separate outlet valve to the atmosphere. From the text take V0 = 0 for parts (a,b), chamber gas is ideal monatomic and isothermal at Ta, and cylinder compression/expansion is adiabatic. Write dN/dt = -P(t)R/(k Ta) and P(t)V = N k Ta, giving dP/dt = -(R/V)P and hence P(t)=Pa exp(-Rt/V). For the emitted gas, note that gas enters the cylinder at pressure P(t) and temperature Ta, then is compressed adiabatically until the outlet opens at Pa. Use T P^{(1-gamma)/gamma}=constant, with gamma=5/3 for monatomic gas, so Tout/Ta=(Pa/P(t))^{(gamma-1)/gamma}=exp(2Rt/5V). method.method_draft: Use a per-stroke discrete cycle map, then take the small-stroke continuous limit. From the image identify one piston cycle as drawing gas from the chamber through the inlet and then exhausting it through the outlet. From the text use V0=0 initially and Delta V << V. During one intake stroke the pump removes from the chamber the number of moles that would occupy Delta V at the current chamber pressure Pn and temperature Ta. Therefore the chamber pressure after one stroke satisfies P_{n+1}V = P_n(V-Delta V), or P_{n+1}=P_n(1-Delta V/V). If the cycle time is tau=Delta V/R, then after n=t/tau cycles, P(t)=Pa(1-Delta V/V)^{Rt/Delta V}, which becomes Pa exp(-Rt/V) for Delta V << V. raw_record.original_question:
A vacuum system consists of a chamber of volume $V$ connected to a vacuum pump. The pump is a cylinder with a piston that moves, with a minimum volume $V_0$ and a maximum volume $V_0 + \Delta V$, where $\Delta V \ll V$. The cylinder has an inlet valve that opens when the cylinder pressure is less than the chamber pressure and an outlet valve that opens when the cylinder pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure $P_a$. The piston moves at such a rate that gas compression/expansion is adiabatic during the pumping cycle. The gas in the chamber is ideal monatomic and remains at a fixed temperature $T_a$. Initially assume $V_0 = 0$ and no leaks.

1. a. At $t=0$ the pressure inside the chamber is $P_a$. Find an equation for the pressure at a later time $t$.
2. b. Find an expression for the temperature of the gas as it is emitted from the pump cylinder into the atmosphere. Your answer may depend on time.
3. c. Now consider the case where $0 < V_0 < \Delta V \ll V$. Find an expression for the minimum possible pressure in the chamber, $P_{\text{min}}$.
raw_record.answer:
$P(t) = P_{a} e^{\frac{-Rt}{V}}$
$T_{out}(t) = T_{a} e^{\frac{2Rt}{5V}}$
$P_{\text{min}} = P_{a} \left(1+ \frac{\Delta V}{V_0}\right)^{-\gamma}$
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: The two attached figures show the same vacuum pump system: on the left is the driving mechanism labeled motor, which drives the piston in the middle labeled cylinder through a connecting rod; inside the cylinder there is a piston plate labeled piston. The right side of the cylinder is connected through valves and piping to the large cavity on the right labeled chamber, and the cavity is marked with volume V. Near the right end of the cylinder there are two valve positions, labeled inlet and outlet respectively, where inlet is located at the connection leading to the cavity, and outlet is the exit leading to the outside.
Reasoning: Let R denote the swept volume rate of the pump, that is, the equivalent volume pumped away from the cavity per unit time. First take V0=0 and no leakage. The gas in the cavity maintains temperature Ta and satisfies P(t)V = N k Ta. During time dt, the pump carries away from the cavity gas whose volume under the cavity state is R dt, so the change in molecule number is dN/dt = -P(t)R/(k Ta). From P V = N k Ta, we get V dP/dt = k Ta dN/dt, so dP/dt = -(R/V)P. Combining the initial condition P(0)=Pa gives P(t)=Pa exp(-Rt/V).
For the discharged gas, when it enters the cylinder, the gas pressure is P(t) and the temperature is Ta; then it is adiabatically compressed in the cylinder until the pressure reaches atmospheric pressure Pa, when outlet opens. For a monatomic ideal gas gamma=5/3, the adiabatic relation can be written as T P^((1-gamma)/gamma)=constant, so Tout/Ta = (Pa/P(t))^((gamma-1)/gamma). Substituting P(t)=Pa exp(-Rt/V) and (gamma-1)/gamma=2/5 gives Tout(t)=Ta exp(2Rt/(5V)).
When there is a finite clearance volume 0<V0<Delta V, after the previous discharge ends, gas at pressure Pa is trapped in the clearance volume V0 inside the cylinder. In the next suction stroke, this part of the gas expands adiabatically from V0 to V0+Delta V, and its lowest pressure is Pa [V0/(V0+Delta V)]^gamma. If the cavity pressure is lower than this value, then inlet no longer opens, so the minimum pressure the cavity can reach is Pmin = Pa [V0/(V0+Delta V)]^gamma = Pa(1+Delta V/V0)^(-gamma).
